verdicts.question: What type of roof is present at the site?

verdicts.question: Are there any obstructions on the roof that could affect the solar installation?

The two overhead water tanks visible in the renders sit on a separate, taller lift/stair block between the two roofs, not on the panel roof planes themselves.
verdicts.rationale: Both proposed panel roof areas appear clear in the available photos; nearby tanks are on an adjacent elevated structure rather than directly on the panel roofs.

verdicts.question: What is the angle of the panels? (in degrees)

Only the CAD layout renders (pages 5-7) state 'Roof/Panel Tilt: 7 Degrees,' but that is designer-entered design data, not independent photographic evidence.
verdicts.rationale: No site photo is taken from an angle that would let a slope/tilt be visually estimated; the only supporting source is the designer's own CAD label.

verdicts.question: In case of sloped roof, what is the slope angle of the roof? (in degrees)

verdicts.question: On how many roofs at the site are we installing solar?
verdicts.designer_notes: In the proposed building, we have two roofs available for installation. 1) Corrugated sheet roof (at the SOUTH SIDE of the terrace) with 12 panels. 2) Corrugated sheet roof (at the NORTH SIDE of the terrace) with 4 panels.

verdicts.question: What type of mounting structure is planned?
verdicts.photo_observation: No mounting hardware is visible in any site photo — the terrace roofs (pages 12-13) appear bare with no rails or structure installed, consistent with a pre-construction site. Only the CAD renders (pages 5-7) label the mounting as 'Flush mounted (On mini-rails)'.
verdicts.rationale: Mounting structure has not been installed yet at the time of the site visit, so photos can't confirm the planned mini-rail hardware.

verdicts.question: What is the orientation of the solar panels?
verdicts.designer_notes: 1) Corrugated sheet roof (at the SOUTH SIDE): PV modules are facing SOUTH. 2) Corrugated sheet roof (at the NORTH SIDE): PV modules are facing NORTH.

verdicts.rationale: Orientation is only corroborated by the designer's own CAD compass overlay, not by an independently verifiable feature in the real site photos.

verdicts.question: How can the roof be accessed?

verdicts.rationale: Multiple dedicated staircase photos with explicit captions directly confirm staircase access to the roof/terrace.

verdicts.question: Is the building currently under construction?

verdicts.question: What is the height of the building and how many floors does it have?

verdicts.rationale: The lane looks narrow and heavy items require manual wall-lifting per the caption, so it's unclear from the photo alone whether a van can reach a true 'unloading point' at the building versus parking on the street.

verdicts.question: Are there any obstacles at the site that could hinder material lifting?
verdicts.photo_observation: Pages 8-10 document an 800mm-wide interior staircase, a route where heavy panels must be shifted over a side wall rather than carried inside, and a ladder climb (page 10) to reach the upper terrace platform.
verdicts.rationale: The documented routes (narrow stairs, wall-lift for heavy items, ladder climb) show real handling complexity; whether this counts as an 'obstacle' is a judgment call best left to a human reviewer.

verdicts.question: Is the cable routing in the site photos continuous and consistent across the documented run — from rooftop panels to DCDB to inverter to ACDB to solar meter to main panel — with no orphan ends, no unexplained mid-run size changes, and visible conduit / cable-tie / clipping where the run is exposed?
verdicts.designer_notes: No designer answer for this target — the vision routine verifies it by tracing cables across photos with 'Cable Routing', 'Equipment Location', 'Meter Box' and similar captions on pages 4+.
verdicts.photo_observation: Page 13: DC cable (red) and DC earthing cable (green) run over the parapet wall connecting the two roof base structures. Page 14: the DC cable enters a narrow room through a drilled hole into a switch box, then a conduit carries it down to the ground-floor LT panel. Pages 15-16: LA (orange) and DC earthing (green) cables run down the building's west side alongside plumbing pipe clamps, reach the ground floor, and are pulled through an existing conduit to the earth pit area, where captions note 'Three earth pits already dug.' Page 17: the run terminates in the ground-floor equipment room labeled DC-DB/Inverter/AC-DB, Main Meter, Solar Meter, AC/DC Earth Pit, LA Pit, UPS Point, and Battery — matching the page 4 cable-routing legend.
verdicts.rationale: Each routing photo picks up exactly where the previous one left off (roof → switch box → conduit → earthing route → earth pits → equipment room), with captions explicitly confirming continuity and conduit entry points at every transition — no orphan ends or unexplained gaps.
